source.title: Avoiding The Double Descent Phenomenon of Random Feature Models Using Hybrid Regularization
source.authors: Kelvin K. Kan; J. Nagy; Lars Ruthotto

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test error across random-feature model widths and training time, and tests regularization as a way to alter the observed curves. Its experiments use random feature models on image datasets rather than deep networks.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own random-feature experiments. Results cited from prior work are not included. Figure-only curves are recorded as figure-only; the paper does not report a training-sample-size sweep.
record.test_reason: The paper reruns a width sweep of min-norm least-squares random-feature models on MNIST and CIFAR10, close to the RFM setup in Belkin et al. (arXiv:1812.11118). It reports the test-error peak at m = n and its descent past it. It then reports early stopping, weight decay and a GCV-tuned hybrid method removing the peak, which bears on V6. Gradient-flow time curves at m = n bear partly on V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that RFM double descent stems from the ill-posedness of the least-squares training problem. Early stopping or weight decay can remove it only with good hyperparameters, which they tuned on test data. Their GCV-based hybrid LSQR method avoids the peak automatically, without validation data. It reaches test error comparable to those test-tuned baselines, including at the interpolation threshold.
record.recipe_differences: The paper sweeps random-feature width and measures least-squares test error, using ReLU random features on MNIST and CIFAR10 with 1,024 training examples. The exact original experimental recipe is not stated here.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different optimal gradient-flow stopping times and weight-decay parameters across datasets; hybrid results vary with iteration count and model width.

fits_no_version.finding: At m = n the smallest singular values of the feature matrix plummet while |u_j^T c| stays flat. This inflates the weight norm, which spikes together with test error. Away from m = n the problem is not ill-posed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The model-wise double-descent peak in least-squares random-feature models is caused by ill-conditioning (vanishing small singular values) of the feature matrix at the interpolation threshold.

record.problems: The experiments use two image datasets and 1,024 training examples. Most curves are presented only in figures; uncertainty across the 5 random trials is not reported. Test data are used to optimize the classical regularization baselines.

untested.parts: All of it; only random-feature models are used, no deep networks.
Epoch-wise curves in deep networks, and at widths other than m = n.
All of it; n is fixed at 1024 and there is no sample-size sweep.
Model classes other than ReLU random-feature least squares.
All of it. Ill-posedness is offered as an explanation of the width peak, but no single complexity measure is tested across size, time and samples.
Label-noise or variance dependence, and multiple or triple peaks.

missing.what: Weight-norm and training-error curves across width: weight norm spikes at m = n and training error is near zero there.
Picard plot singular-value decay at m = 512, 1024 and 2048, showing ill-posedness only at m = n.
Weight-decay sweep over α at m = n: test error first falls then grows with α. The optimal α differs by about 10x between datasets.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's main aim is mitigation, but it reports the unregularized curve, so it counts as a test. Belkin et al. also used random-feature least squares, so the V4 replication is near-T1, with ReLU features and CIFAR10 as the differences. Most curves are figure-only, with 5 trials and no spread reported. Hybrid and LSQR iteration curves are regularized-method curves and were relinked from V2 to V6.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use random feature models, not deep networks.
The paper tests gradient-flow time at m = n and hybrid LSQR iterations; it does not test other training procedures or a general range of training-time settings.
The model class tested is random feature models; other model classes are not tested.
The paper discusses ill-posedness and singular values but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.

The paper tests regularization effects, but not whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether peaks split into multiple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates peaks across model classes.
No effective-parameter count is used to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
